cse-2021-2-cs-2.approach: In a min-heap the maximum must be a leaf, and the leaves are the last $\lceil n/2 \rceil$ array cells with no order among them, so all of them must be examined.

steps.title: Max is a leaf
steps.body: Every internal node is smaller than its children, so an internal node can never be the maximum. In an array heap the leaves are indices $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor + 1, \ldots, n$ — about $n/2$ elements.

steps.title: All leaves must be checked
steps.body: The heap property says nothing about the order of leaves, so any one of them could be the maximum. Scanning $\lceil n/2 \rceil$ leaves costs $\Theta(n)$, and no algorithm can skip one (an adversary makes the skipped leaf the largest). So the optimal worst case is $\Theta(n)$.

optionAnalysis.reason: $\Theta(1)$ is the cost of finding the **minimum** (the root), not the maximum.
$\Theta(\log n)$ would follow a single root-to-leaf path, but the max can lie under any branch.
Correct: about $n/2$ unordered leaves must be scanned.
$\Theta(n\log n)$ is the cost of heapsort — far more than needed.

cse-2021-2-cs-2.verification: Example: heap $[1,2,3,9,4,5,6]$ — the max 9 is a leaf at index 4, found only by scanning the leaves 4..7.
